answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (i.e. create a Cosmos DB "database account").

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group in the core Azure CLI. Example: az cosmosdb create --name <account> --resource-group <rg> --kind MongoDB.

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep: resource of type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform (azurerm): resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" (provider azurerm) with kind = "MongoDB".

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: MongoDB-style URI. Example form I would use: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&authSource=admin. (Scheme mongodb:// or mongodb+srv:// on SRV-supporting endpoints; host suffix .mongo.cosmos.azure.com, default TLS port 10255 for non-SRV endpoints; require ssl=true and often retryWrites=false and replicaSet=globaldb.)

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Primary billing model is Cosmos DB style throughput: provisioned RU/s (or autoscale RU/s) or serverless (RU consumption). There are also dedicated instance/compute tier offerings in some SKUs, but the standard model to plan for is RU/s (request units/sec) and serverless options.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: For the MongoDB-compatible API you authenticate with MongoDB-style credentials (database users / SCRAM username:password). The Cosmos account keys (primary/master keys) and resource tokens are used for Cosmos SQL API; Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) authentication is not generally used for the MongoDB wire protocol endpoints. In short: use MongoDB user credentials (SCRAM) from the driver; Azure AD integration is for other Cosmos APIs and not the primary Mongo endpoint.

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: For MongoDB API workloads use standard MongoDB drivers (e.g. pymongo for Python, mongodb node driver). There is an azure-cosmos SDK but that is for the SQL/Core API — not for Mongo-compatible endpoints. So for this sample use pymongo / motor / official MongoDB drivers.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: I expect provider-supported vector indexes include HNSW and IVF (and possibly DiskANN) exposed via an extended createIndex option. Example command I'd run (best-effort): db.patient_chunks.createIndex({embedding: 'vector'}, {vector: {algorithm: 'hnsw', similarity: 'cosine', dims: 1536, m:16, efConstruction:200}}). Note: this is an engine-specific extended createIndex syntax, not standard Mongo; you must supply the index type and parameters in the createIndex options.

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: There isn't a first-class MongoDB Atlas-style full-text/hybrid search built into the Mongo API; typical approach on Azure is to integrate with Azure Cognitive Search (indexing data via change feed or connectors). For vector+text hybrid search you either use the provider's vector indexes if available (see Q08) or export data into Azure Cognitive Search or an external vector search engine and perform hybrid ranking there.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Expect compatibility tiers that map to MongoDB server versions (commonly supported: 3.6/4.0/4.2/4.4 and more recent accounts may advertise 5.x/6.x compatibility). Some MongoDB server features are limited or unsupported (server-side JavaScript, certain aggregation stages or operators, some admin commands, some transactional or change-stream behaviors depending on the compatibility level). Plan to verify the exact server version advertised by the account and test any advanced features you rely on.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is no official Mongo API emulator for Cosmos that fully reproduces the managed service. For local development use a local MongoDB docker image (e.g. mongo:6.0) and bind port 27017. Example: docker run --rm -p 27017:27017 --name local-mongo -d mongo:6.0. Then point pymongo at mongodb://localhost:27017 for local testing.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: For the MongoDB API change streams historically were not fully supported; Cosmos DB has its own Change Feed mechanism on the SQL API. If you need change-stream-like behavior you either must use the provider's change feed API or verify that the account's MongoDB compatibility level explicitly advertises change stream support. In short: don't assume MongoDB change streams are available unless the specific account/compatibility level documents support for them.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the documentdb MCP server (i.e. MCP server named "documentdb") for data-plane inspection tooling for this service. The general Azure MCP server does not provide the same Mongo/Cosmos-specific index/collection inspection commands; you need the documentdb-specific MCP server profile.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Originally Microsoft named the service DocumentDB; it was later rebranded as Azure Cosmos DB (Cosmos). The "MongoDB-compatible" surface is an API layer on top of the Cosmos engine. This Microsoft DocumentDB/Cosmos service is distinct from Amazon DocumentDB and from any unrelated open-source project called DocumentDB; they are separate implementations.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Under the Mongo-compatible surface sits the provider's proprietary storage/engine (Cosmos engine) that translates Mongo wire protocol operations into its internal operations. That means standard Mongo drivers usually work, but expect differences in supported commands, performance characteristics, consistency semantics, indexing behavior and some missing Mongo features. Application-level code should stick to widely-used driver APIs and test any advanced Mongo-specific features.

answers.question: What index definition does this sample need for vector search?
answers.answer: Create a vector index on the embedding field with HNSW params. Example I would run in the Mongo shell (engine-extended createIndex): db.patient_chunks.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'embedding_hnsw', vector: { algorithm: 'hnsw', similarity: 'cosine', dims: 1536, m: 16, efConstruction: 200 } });

answers.question: How do I create the application collection with patientId as the partition key / access-control key?
answers.answer: Create a collection named patient_chunks in database sample_healthcare_01 and ensure an index on patientId. Example (mongo shell): use sample_healthcare_01; db.createCollection('patient_chunks'); db.patient_chunks.createIndex({ patientId: 1 }); For sharded/partitioned Cosmos accounts you may also need to define the partition key at collection creation; in Mongo API this maps to ensuring patientId is the shard key.

answers.question: How should the Python app connect to the cluster reading DOCUMENTDB_URI?
answers.answer: Use pymongo and read os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']. Example code: from pymongo import MongoClient; import os; uri = os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']; client = MongoClient(uri, tls=True); db = client['sample_healthcare_01']; collection = db['patient_chunks']. Ensure the URI includes ssl=true and authSource=admin if required.

answers.question: What vector index creation command will the sample try to run to verify vector support?
answers.answer: The sample will attempt an engine-extended createIndex call like: db.patient_chunks.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'embedding_index', vector: { algorithm: 'hnsw', similarity: 'cosine', dims: 1536 } }); If that fails, fall back to storing embeddings and calling a provider-specific vector search API or external vector index.

answers.question: How should we enforce patientId-based access control in this sample?
answers.answer: Enforce access control at the application layer: authenticate the requester (e.g. via your app's auth), then always add patientId equality to any query (e.g. collection.find({ patientId: allowed_patient_id, ...other_filters })). Do not rely on Mongo user-level per-document enforcement; instead use scoped queries and validate patientId on every operation. For admin tasks create a separate management user with broader rights.
